The Fracklebelly madtom Noturus munitus is a diminutive ictalurid catfish endemic to the upper Mobile Bay Basin, where it inhabits shallow, swift-flowing gravel shoals. Adults of this species reach a maximum standard length of 7.7 centimeters [Li = 7.7 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds to a total length of approximately 9.5 cm based on morphometric relationships from preserved specimens. This relatively small ultimate size places N. munitus among the smaller members of its genus, a trait that likely influences its overall life-history strategy. Field surveys conducted during the spring spawning season indicate that sexual maturation is initiated once individuals attain a standard length at puberty of 4.1 centimeters [Lp = 4.1 centimeters]; this critical size threshold was confirmed by the dissection of a gravid female measuring 4.1 cm SL that contained 55 developing oocytes, providing a clear empirical basis for the onset of reproductive capacity. The transition to maturity at such a modest body length suggests that this species may prioritize early reproduction, a common pattern in small-bodied stream fishes facing high adult mortality from unpredictable flow regimes and predation.

Neonatal body size in the Fracklebelly madtom is extraordinarily small, reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo. Based on a mean egg diameter of 2.8 millimeters reported for the closely related yellowfin madtom Noturus flavipinnis, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0115 grams [Wwb = 0.0115 grams], a value derived from the volumetric formula for a sphere using the average egg diameter. This minute birth mass places newly hatched larvae among the smallest of any North American ictalurid, a condition that imposes a brief period of dependence on endogenous yolk reserves before exogenous feeding must commence. Hatchlings emerge as non-feeding, yolk-sac larvae, relying entirely on their yolk stores for early development and somatic growth. The transition to the onset of exogenous feeding occurs rapidly, as the yolk is absorbed within the first few days post-eclosion, after which the larvae must successfully capture small aquatic invertebrates to sustain further growth and avoid starvation.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], reproductive output in Noturus munitus has been characterized with considerable precision. Females produce an average of 55 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 55 eggs per spawning event], and an individual can complete a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], reflecting an iteroparous reproductive strategy that is typical of madtom catfishes in temperate streams. This combination of moderate fecundity and infrequent spawning suggests that the annual reproductive output is constrained by the energetic costs of egg production and the availability of suitable nesting cavities under stable gravel substrates. The maximum reproductive rate is thus achieved when females successfully spawn a single clutch annually, ensuring that each reproductive effort receives adequate maternal investment in yolk provisioning to maximize larval survival. The extended developmental period at this temperature allows for efficient yolk conversion and gradual larval growth before the onset of winter conditions.

As females approach the upper end of the size distribution, their total wet body mass increases predictably with length according to a length–weight relationship established for the species. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum recorded body mass for a fully grown adult, is 6.2 grams [Wwi = 6.2 grams], derived from the allometric equation 0.00575 multiplied by the standard length raised to the power of 3.10. This asymptotic mass is modest even by madtom standards and underscores the species’ overall small body size throughout its life history. The relationship between length and mass indicates that growth is slightly positively allometric, meaning that larger individuals are proportionally heavier than would be expected from isometric scaling, possibly reflecting greater reproductive tissue development or lipid storage in mature females. Field-caught specimens approaching this maximum mass are typically gravid females collected during the late spring breeding season, suggesting that the energetic investment in egg production drives much of the late-life mass accumulation.

Longevity data for the Fracklebelly madtom, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith microchemistry analysis, indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural thermal regimes approximates 4.5 years [am = 4.5 years] when evaluated at a baseline water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, equivalent to approximately 1642 days, is consistent with the life-history strategy of a small, fast-maturing ictalurid occupying a dynamic lotic environment with seasonal flood pulses. Mortality is highest during the first year of life, particularly during the larval drift and early juvenile stages when predation by larger fish and aquatic insects is intense. Individuals that survive to reproductive age often experience senescence-related declines in body condition and fecundity during their fourth year, with few individuals persisting beyond the fifth year of life. The combination of early maturity at a small size and a compressed lifespan reinforces the view of Noturus munitus as an r-selected species adapted to unpredictable stream habitats.
